patient.name: Bernard Okwuosa
patient.chief_complaint: Bilateral leg weakness and numbness worsening over 4 months, cannot climb stairs
patient.hpi: Bernard Okwuosa is a 62-year-old retired high school principal with a 4-month history of progressive bilateral lower extremity weakness and numbness that has not responded to pregabalin initiated by his primary care physician. He was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes 8 years ago, and his primary care physician attributed his current symptoms to diabetic peripheral neuropathy. However, his neurologist notes several features atypical for diabetic neuropathy: the weakness is prominent and proximal as well as distal, the course has been rapidly progressive over only 4 months rather than the gradual years-long progression of diabetic neuropathy, and his right upper extremity has recently become involved with hand weakness and difficulty opening jars. He reports bilateral foot and calf numbness and tingling beginning 4 months ago, followed within 6 weeks by prominent thigh weakness making stair-climbing difficult. He struggles to rise from low chairs and has fallen twice. He reports new right hand weakness over the past 6 weeks. He denies bowel or bladder involvement. His HbA1c has been 7.2% for the past year on metformin and sitagliptin. He has no history of alcohol use, recent travel, or toxic exposures. He denies weight loss. A prior NCS performed by his primary care physician 3 years ago showed mild axonal changes attributed to diabetes. He is now referred to neurology for progressive weakness not fitting diabetic neuropathy.

results.NCS_interpretation: MIXED DEMYELINATING AND AXONAL POLYNEUROPATHY with CONDUCTION BLOCK. Velocity reductions exceed what is expected for axonal loss alone in diabetic neuropathy (LLN should be ~40 m/s; found 36-38 m/s). Conduction block present at non-entrapment sites (across popliteal segment bilateral). Proximal EMG involvement. Pattern is INCONSISTENT with length-dependent diabetic axonal neuropathy. Findings support CIDP superimposed on pre-existing mild diabetic axonal neuropathy.

followup_outputs.interpretation: Nerve conduction study shows mixed demyelinating-axonal pattern with conduction block at non-compressive sites and proximal EMG involvement. This is the hallmark of CIDP, not pure diabetic neuropathy.

followup_outputs.special_stains: Gram stain negative; India ink negative
followup_outputs.interpretation: Markedly elevated CSF protein at 118 mg/dL with normal cell count — classic albumino-cytologic dissociation of CIDP. No infectious or malignant etiology. CSF protein elevation of this degree (>80 mg/dL) in the setting of demyelinating NCS confirms CIDP diagnosis. Note: diabetic neuropathy typically has normal or only mildly elevated CSF protein (<60 mg/dL).

followup_outputs.indication: Confirm CIDP histopathology; exclude vasculitis, amyloid, or other causes

findings.Gross: 1.8 cm sural nerve segment, grossly normal.
findings.Light_microscopy: SEGMENTAL DEMYELINATION AND REMYELINATION with ONION BULB FORMATIONS (concentric Schwann cell processes wrapping around single axon — hallmark of repeated demyelination). Moderate endoneurial fibrosis. Patchy mononuclear inflammatory infiltrate (CD8+ T cells and macrophages) in endoneurium and perineurium. Macrophage-associated demyelination present.
findings.Axonal_density: Moderate reduction in large myelinated fiber density (~35% reduction from age-matched controls). Unmyelinated fiber density mildly reduced.
findings.Vasculitis: ABSENT — no epineurial or endoneurial vasculitis. Vessel walls intact.
findings.Electron_microscopy: Widely-spaced myelin lamellae NOT present (anti-MAG pattern excluded). Redundant myelin loops. Onion bulbs confirmed.
findings.Immunofluorescence: No IgG, IgA, IgM, or complement deposits on myelin.

followup_outputs.interpretation: Sural nerve biopsy confirms CIDP: segmental demyelination, onion bulb formations, and macrophage-associated demyelination with T-cell infiltrate. No vasculitis, amyloid, or anti-MAG widely-spaced myelin lamellae. Axonal loss is moderate, consistent with chronic CIDP with secondary axonal degeneration. This is superimposed on background mild diabetic axonal neuropathy.

results.title: CIDP in diabetic patients: frequency, clinical features, and treatment response
results.key_finding: CIDP occurs more frequently in diabetic patients (11x age-adjusted rate). Distinguishing features from diabetic neuropathy: proximal weakness, motor involvement, elevated CSF protein >80 mg/dL, demyelinating NCS with conduction block. IVIG response rate 70-80% in CIDP+diabetes.

results.title: Conduction block and temporal dispersion in CIDP: diagnostic criteria update
results.key_finding: EAN/PNS 2021 CIDP diagnostic criteria require: definite conduction block (>50% CMAP amplitude drop) OR probable conduction block (30-50% drop) at non-compressive sites, OR demyelinating velocities with elevated CSF protein. Conduction block at popliteal segment (non-compressive) is a valid diagnostic finding.

results.title: MRI nerve root enhancement as a diagnostic biomarker for CIDP
results.key_finding: Gadolinium enhancement of spinal nerve roots and cauda equina has 62% sensitivity and 95% specificity for CIDP. Enhancement of posterior nerve roots is particularly specific. This finding supports CIDP diagnosis when NCS criteria are borderline.

interactions.description: IVIG may cause transient glucose fluctuations due to sucrose or glucose stabilizers in some formulations. Monitor blood glucose during and 24-48 hours after IVIG infusion. Consider sucrose-free IVIG formulations (e.g., Gammagard Liquid, Privigen) in diabetic patients.
No significant interaction. IVIG does not affect statin metabolism.

followup_outputs.contraindications: IgA level 284 mg/dL — IVIG is safe (IgA deficiency excluded). No contraindications to IVIG identified.
followup_outputs.recommendations: Use sucrose-free IVIG formulation for this diabetic patient. Monitor glucose during infusion. Renal function (eGFR 68) adequate for IVIG — no dose adjustment required.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (CIDP) superimposed on mild diabetic axonal polyneuropathy
key_findings: Mixed demyelinating-axonal NCS with conduction block at non-compressive sites (popliteal segment) in bilateral peroneal and tibial nerves
Velocities 36-38 m/s (slowing beyond typical diabetic axonal) with conduction block
Proximal EMG involvement: vastus lateralis, iliopsoas fibrillations — not length-dependent
CSF albumino-cytologic dissociation: protein 118 mg/dL, WBC 2/uL
MRI bilateral cauda equina and posterior nerve root gadolinium enhancement
Sural nerve biopsy: segmental demyelination + onion bulbs + macrophage-associated demyelination, NO vasculitis
IgA 284 mg/dL — IVIG safe; anti-NF155/CNTN1 negative — standard CIDP (not nodopathy)
Well-controlled diabetes HbA1c 7.2% with mild prior axonal NCS 3 years ago — CIDP is the new superimposed process
Rapid 4-month progression with upper extremity involvement atypical for diabetic neuropathy alone
critical_actions: IVIG 2 g/kg over 2-5 days induction (IgA safe); use sucrose-free formulation in diabetic patient
IVIG maintenance 1 g/kg every 3-4 weeks (assess response at 3 months)
Monitor NCS at 6 months to document treatment response
Continue diabetes management; HbA1c optimization reduces axonal component
If IVIG fails at 6 months: consider oral prednisone taper or subcutaneous immunoglobulin (SCIG)
pitfalls: Attributing all symptoms to well-controlled diabetes (HbA1c 7.2% — too good to cause this severity)
Missing conduction block at popliteal segment (non-entrapment site diagnostic for CIDP)
Skipping CSF — the albumino-cytologic dissociation (protein 118) is key diagnostic confirmation
Not checking IgA before IVIG (IVIG contraindicated in IgA deficiency — must always check)
Missing MRI nerve root enhancement which provides supportive evidence when NCS borderline
Not distinguishing anti-NF155/CNTN1 nodopathy (IVIG-refractory) from standard CIDP

optimal_actions.action: interpret_labs (CBC, CMP, HbA1c, B12, SPEP, immunofixation, anti-MAG, paraneoplastic panel)
interpret_labs (NCS/EMG with conduction block testing — proximal segments bilateral)

teaching_points: CIDP is 11x more common in diabetic patients — always consider when neuropathy is atypical (proximal weakness, rapid progression, upper extremity involvement)
Conduction block at non-entrapment sites (popliteal, mid-thigh) is pathognomonic for CIDP
CSF albumino-cytologic dissociation (high protein, normal cells) is the cardinal CSF feature of CIDP
MRI nerve root and cauda equina gadolinium enhancement has 95% specificity for CIDP
Always check IgA before IVIG — contraindicated in IgA deficiency (<7 mg/dL)
Anti-NF155/CNTN1 negative = standard CIDP, likely IVIG-responsive; positive = nodopathy variant, IVIG-refractory
Sucrose-free IVIG formulations preferred in diabetic patients to avoid hyperglycemic episodes
